# Build notes — issue #1801

## State at start of this call

Previous test stage found 3 failures:
1. runner-job-control-abort-test.sh — "flag-on: monitor mode ON in runner shell" (got: dash=huB)
2. runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh — SPEC-6b (pid still alive 5s after runner returned)
3. stage-timeout-dispatch-test.sh — SPEC-10 (kill -KILL still present)

## What I found

Running tests on current tree at start of this iteration:
- stage-timeout-dispatch-test.sh: ALL PASS (SPEC-10 already fixed in prior iteration)
- runner-job-control-abort-test.sh: ALL PASS (flag-on check already fixed in prior iteration)
- runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh: SPEC-5 FAILS with empty marker, SPEC-6b PASSES

## Root cause of SPEC-5 failure (refined analysis)

The initial fix (adding `trap "" TERM` before `_runner_signal_trap TERM`) was WRONG because
`trap "" TERM` was placed AFTER the zbuild_pg_kill calls, which contain `sleep 0.1` loops.

The actual bug is BASH TRAP RE-ENTRY. In bash, when a foreground command (like `sleep 0.1`)
is running inside a trap body, and a second TERM signal arrives, bash delivers the second TERM
when `sleep 0.1` exits - EVEN THOUGH we're already in a TERM trap handler. This re-enters
the trap body.

With SPEC-5's process-group kill:
1. TERM sent to process group: both runner and `timeout 120` receive TERM simultaneously
2. Runner's lifecycle TERM trap fires (first instance)
3. `zbuild_pg_kill "$_lc_hook_pid" 1` runs: internally loops `sleep 0.1` up to 10 times
4. During one of these sleeps, `timeout 120` (which also received TERM) sends TERM to runner
5. When `sleep 0.1` exits, bash delivers the second TERM: TRAP RE-ENTRY!
6. Second trap instance runs: kills hook/wd, `_runner_signal_trap TERM` → `exit 1` → EXIT trap starts
7. EXIT trap: `_runner_dispatch_always_run` starts cleanup
8. First trap instance resumes: `_runner_signal_trap TERM` → `exit 1` INSIDE the EXIT trap
9. `exit 1` inside EXIT trap = immediate termination, aborting cleanup
10. RELEASE_MARKER is never written

Confirmed by experiment: bash DOES re-enter TERM traps when a second TERM arrives during
a foreground command (`sleep`) inside the first trap body.

## Fix applied (revised)

Move `trap "" TERM` to the VERY BEGINNING of both trap bodies (subshell and main-shell).
This prevents any re-entry: the first thing the trap does is ignore further TERMs.

Change: lifecycle.sh TERM trap for both subshell and main-shell cases:
- Before (subshell): `trap 'zbuild_pg_kill ...; exit 143' TERM`
- After  (subshell): `trap 'trap "" TERM; zbuild_pg_kill ...; exit 143' TERM`
- Before (main):     `trap 'zbuild_pg_kill ...; zbuild_pg_kill ...; trap "" TERM; ...' TERM`
- After  (main):     `trap 'trap "" TERM; zbuild_pg_kill ...; zbuild_pg_kill ...; ...' TERM`

## Why this doesn't break SPEC-6b

SPEC-6b: cleanup hook spawns TERM-ignoring child, calls `wait`. Always_run watchdog sends
TERM to plugin_hook_call's subshell group. With `trap "" TERM` at the start of the subshell
trap:
1. TERM arrives, `trap "" TERM` fires immediately (prevents re-entry)
2. `zbuild_pg_kill "$_lc_hook_pid" 1` - sends TERM to hook group, then KILL after 1s
3. The TERM-ignoring child is in the same group (set +m in hook subshell), gets KILLed
4. `exit 143`

SPEC-6b should still pass because zbuild_pg_kill sends KILL (which can't be ignored).

## Tests verified this iteration

1. stage-timeout-dispatch-test.sh: ALL PASS (confirmed after fix)
2. runner-job-control-abort-test.sh: ALL PASS (confirmed after fix)
3. runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh: RUNNING IN BACKGROUND (waiting for result)

            # them. If the caller had set -m (e.g. _runner_dispatch_always_run's

            # their own groups, escaping the KILL (#2333 SPEC-6b).

        #     the runner process (sequential / roleless dispatch).  We kill the
        #     hook group, then delegate to the runner's own signal handler

        #     normally (emits pipeline.aborted, exits 1).  Fall back to

            # arrives while a foreground command inside the trap body is running

            # starting a second instance of this body.

        else

            # `trap "" TERM` FIRST: same re-entry guard as the subshell case.
            # A process-group kill (e.g. SPEC-5's `kill -TERM -PGID`) delivers
            # TERM to the runner AND to any process in the same group (e.g.
            # `timeout 120`).  `timeout` forwards TERM to the runner before
            # exiting, producing a second TERM.  Without the early ignore the
            # second TERM interrupts the zbuild_pg_kill sleep loops, re-enters
            # this trap body, and calls `exit 1` inside the EXIT trap's teardown,
            # aborting it before the release marker is written (SPEC-5 failure).

# kill through zbuild_pg_kill; no hand-rolled TERM/KILL sequence remains for
# stage dispatch.

# watchdog there covers every route. These tests FAIL on pre-change code

# ─── [#1801/SPEC-1] every dispatch route reaches plugin_hook_call ─────────────
print_test_section "[#1801/SPEC-1] all dispatch routes lead through plugin_hook_call"

# The design states: all dispatch routes — map, fanout, sequential strategy,
# roleless leaf, cycle member, parallel-group member, always_run — reach
# plugin_hook_call. Verify that each strategy file and the runner itself calls
# plugin_hook_call (not a private bypass).
for _sf in \
    core/pipeline/strategies/fanout.sh \
    core/pipeline/strategies/sequential.sh \
    core/pipeline/strategies/map.sh \

    else

    fi

# ─── [#1801/SPEC-1] specific named routes: cycle member, parallel-group member, roleless leaf ──
# runner.sh hosts three explicit dispatch routes that all must reach plugin_hook_call:
#   cycle_dispatch_stage      — cycle member (calls plugin_hook_call for each member/iteration)
#   parallel_dispatch_stage   — parallel-group member (concurrent per-member dispatch)
#   roleless leaf             — direct dispatch when the template has no roles (backward compat)
# Each is explicitly verified below so a refactor that moves one of them out of lifecycle.sh
# without updating the watchdog would cause these assertions to fail.

_runner="$REPO_ROOT/core/pipeline/runner.sh"

# cycle member — extract function body (4-space indented in runner.sh)
_cycle_fn_body=""
if [[ -f "$_runner" ]]; then
    _cycle_fn_body="$(awk '/^    cycle_dispatch_stage\(\) \{/{p=1} p{print} p && /^    \}$/{p=0;exit}' "$_runner" 2>/dev/null || true)"
fi
if grep -q 'plugin_hook_call' <<< "$_cycle_fn_body"; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-1] cycle member: cycle_dispatch_stage in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-1] cycle member: cycle_dispatch_stage in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call" \
        "plugin_hook_call not found inside cycle_dispatch_stage — cycle members bypass the per-dispatch watchdog"
fi

# parallel-group member — extract function body
_parallel_fn_body=""
if [[ -f "$_runner" ]]; then
    _parallel_fn_body="$(awk '/^    parallel_dispatch_stage\(\) \{/{p=1} p{print} p && /^    \}$/{p=0;exit}' "$_runner" 2>/dev/null || true)"
fi
if grep -q 'plugin_hook_call' <<< "$_parallel_fn_body"; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-1] parallel-group member: parallel_dispatch_stage in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-1] parallel-group member: parallel_dispatch_stage in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call" \
        "plugin_hook_call not found inside parallel_dispatch_stage — parallel members bypass the per-dispatch watchdog"
fi

# always_run route — AWK-extract _runner_dispatch_always_run body and confirm it calls plugin_hook_call.
# SPEC-1 requires this to be established via body extraction, not a file-level grep on runner.sh,
# so that a refactor moving the dispatch call out of the function cannot slip through.
_always_run_fn_body=""
if [[ -f "$_runner" ]]; then
    _always_run_fn_body="$(awk '/_runner_dispatch_always_run\(\) \{/{p=1} p{print} p && /^    \}$/{exit}' "$_runner" 2>/dev/null || true)"
fi
if grep -q 'plugin_hook_call' <<< "$_always_run_fn_body"; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-1] always_run route: _runner_dispatch_always_run in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-1] always_run route: _runner_dispatch_always_run in runner.sh calls plugin_hook_call" \
        "plugin_hook_call not found inside _runner_dispatch_always_run body — always_run stages bypass the per-dispatch watchdog"
fi

# roleless leaf — the path taken when the stage has no template roles (backward-compat direct dispatch)
# In runner.sh: if [[ -z "$roles_out" ]] … plugin_hook_call … else (strategy dispatch)
# runner.sh has MULTIPLE occurrences of `[[ -z "$roles_out" ]]`: the first is a dry-run
# display block that does NOT call plugin_hook_call. The dispatch-path occurrence does.
# We scan ALL occurrences, capturing up to 40 lines after each, and check whether ANY
# captured window contains plugin_hook_call — so the dry-run block cannot mask the real hit.
_roleless_found=0
if [[ -f "$_runner" ]]; then
    _roleless_found="$(awk '
        /\[\[ -z "\$roles_out" \]\]/ { block=40 }
        block > 0 {
            if (/plugin_hook_call/) { found=1; exit }
            block--
        }
        END { print found+0 }
    ' "$_runner" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"
fi
if [[ "$_roleless_found" -eq 1 ]]; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-1] roleless leaf: direct plugin_hook_call when template has no roles"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-1] roleless leaf: direct plugin_hook_call when template has no roles" \
        "plugin_hook_call not found within 40 lines of any '[[ -z \"\$roles_out\" ]]' check — roleless stages bypass the watchdog"
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# [#1801/SPEC-3] stage_timeout_s precedence: template value beats
# ZBUILD_STAGE_TIMEOUT_S beats the 5400 s engine default, each tier
# verified in isolation.
#
# These tests FAIL on pre-change code (where stage_timeout_s is not a
# recognized template field and _TPL_STAGE_TIMEOUT_S_* is never exported)
# and PASS after the change.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/../.." && pwd)"

# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/helpers.sh
source "$REPO_ROOT/scripts/lib/helpers.sh"
# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/test-helpers.sh

_MINIMAL_HEAD='id: t

  strategy: fanout

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lib/proc-group.sh — process-group resolution and kill helpers.
# Extracted from core/router/route.sh (Wave 15-G, #687) so the test stage and
# any other long-running spawn share one implementation (#1748).
# Sourced library: no set -euo pipefail.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED=1

# #2056: there is no setsid prefix any more. Process groups come from `set -m`
# at the spawn site — bash job control makes a backgrounded job a group leader,
# which is POSIX and identical on macOS and Linux.
#
# `setsid -w` was wrong here twice over. It is absent on macOS (util-linux is
# keg-only), so the prefix went empty, no group was created, and an abort
# degraded to a single-PID kill while every descendant survived — the Wave 15-G
# guarantee held on Linux only, and the test covering it is Linux-only too, so
# nothing said so. And `-w` forces setsid to fork, because it waits for the
# child and returns its exit status, so the pid the caller captured was the
# wrapper rather than the new session leader.
#
# Do not reintroduce a prefix here. A spawn that needs an external binary to get
# a process group is a spawn whose guarantee is platform-conditional.

# Prints the PGID safe to signal for <pid>, or nothing. Empty is not "no group":
# it means the group could not be proven distinct from ours, and signalling it
# would take down the runner itself — so callers must fall back to a PID kill.
zbuild_pg_resolve() {
    local _pid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    local _child _self
    _child="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    if [[ -n "$_child" && -n "$_self" && "$_child" != "$_self" ]]; then
        printf '%s' "$_child"
        return 0
    fi
    # A short-lived child can exit before `ps` reports it. Under `set -m` the
    # spawn IS the group leader, so PGID == PID by construction and that stays
    # true after it is gone — reporting the pid is correct, not a guess.
    #
    # This branch previously justified itself with "setsid execs in place, so it
    # needs no fork". That was false under `-w` (#2056): setsid forks in order to
    # wait, so the captured pid was the wrapper and the group belonged to a
    # process one fork below. Under job control there is no wrapper to be wrong
    # about.
    if [[ -z "$_child" ]]; then
        printf '%s' "$_pid"
    fi
}

# TERM <target>, then KILL whatever is left after <grace_s>. Shared by the group
# and single-PID paths so both get the same grace — the escalation is the whole
# contract, and a caller that skips it is indistinguishable from a plain KILL.
#
# Synchronous by construction (#905): the `{ sleep 1 && kill -KILL; } &` backstop
# this replaces could outlive the caller that armed it, so teardown returned
# while the tree was still alive and the backstop was sometimes lost with it.
# Polling instead costs milliseconds when the target exits on TERM, costs the
# full grace only when it ignores TERM, and leaves nothing running on return.
_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill() {
    # `--` because a group target is spelled `-PGID` and would otherwise parse
    # as an option.
    local _target="$1" _grace="$2"
    kill -TERM -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
    local _ticks=$(( _grace * 10 )) _i=0
    while (( _i < _ticks )); do
        kill -0 -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || return 0
        sleep 0.1 2>/dev/null || true
        _i=$(( _i + 1 ))
    done
    kill -KILL -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
}

# A non-numeric grace would evaluate to 0 in the arithmetic context above, so the
# poll loop would never run and the target would go straight to KILL — silently
# losing the escalation the caller asked for. Clamp to the default instead.
_zbuild_pg_grace() {
    local _g="${1:-1}"
    [[ "$_g" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$_g" -gt 0 ]] && printf '%s' "$_g" || printf '1'
}

# zbuild_pg_record_pgid <file> — the pgid out of a `.pgid` record.
#
# ONE reader, because there are two formats on disk and three places that read
# them (#2018). The engine's dispatch record is `<pgid>\t<leader start time>`;
# tool/test's own `test-stage.pgid` is a bare number; and a record written before
# #2018 is bare too. A reader that only understands one of those does not error —
# it fails the numeric guard and `continue`s, so the caller kills NOTHING and
# reports success. That is how a format change here silently disables ADR-062 §2
# reclamation, which is the path that actually runs on every normal exit.
#
# Prints nothing and returns 1 when there is no usable pgid, so a caller can
# still distinguish "no record" from "record says 1234".
zbuild_pg_record_pgid() {
    local _f="${1:-}" _pgid=""
    [[ -n "$_f" && -f "$_f" ]] || return 1
    IFS=$'\t' read -r _pgid _ 2>/dev/null < "$_f" || true
    [[ "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 1
    printf '%s' "$_pgid"
}

# zbuild_pg_register <pgid> — record a process group the caller just created.
#
# ADR-062 §1 had the ENGINE record this at dispatch. It could not, and the reason
# is structural: a stage is a bash function call, not a subprocess, so at the
# dispatch seam no group exists yet. That code fell back to `$$`'s group — the
# engine's own — which teardown then skipped, correctly, because signalling your
# own group takes the runner down with it. Every record was unkillable, every
# record was skipped, and §2's kill loop never freed anything (#2024).
#
# So the direction reverses: whoever CREATES a group registers it. Two sites do,
# and only two — `tool/test`'s `set -m` suite and the router's `setsid` spawn.
#
# Refusing to register our own group is the invariant, not a safety check. A
# record naming the registrar's own group is strictly worse than no record: it
# cannot be acted on, and it makes the mechanism look live while it does nothing
# — which is exactly how the original defect survived #2001, #2018 and an ADR.
#
# Fail-open throughout: a spawn is never refused because bookkeeping was
# unavailable. Silence here costs a possible leak; failing here costs the run.
zbuild_pg_register() {
    local _pgid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    local _self
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
    local _sd="${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}"
    [[ -n "$_sd" && -d "$_sd" ]] || return 0
    local _stage="${2:-${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}}"
    [[ -n "$_stage" ]] || return 0
    # One path component, sanitised the same way stage scratch keys are, so no
    # stage name can climb out of runtime/.
    _stage="${_stage//[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/_}"
    local _dir="${_sd}/runtime/stages"
    mkdir -p "$_dir" 2>/dev/null || return 0
    # #2018 format: the leader's start time proves the pgid still names what
    # recorded it, so a later sweep cannot signal a recycled pid.
    local _start
    _start="$(ps -o lstart= -p "$_pgid" 2>/dev/null | tr -s ' ' | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' || true)"
    printf '%s\t%s' "$_pgid" "$_start" > "${_dir}/${_stage}.pgid" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}

# TERM then KILL a whole process group. `-PGID` is the negative-pid convention.
zbuild_pg_kill() {
    local _pgid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    # Refuse our own group: `kill -- -PGID` from inside it takes down the runner.
    local _self
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "-$_pgid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
}

# TERM then KILL a single PID — the path taken when no group could be proven.
# It gets the same grace as the group path: a suite that flushes coverage or
# writes partial results on SIGTERM needs the window wherever it is killed from.
zbuild_pid_kill() {
    local _pid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "$_pid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
}

Now I see the issue clearly. The `zbuild_pg_kill` function calls `_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill` which internally calls:
```bash
kill -TERM -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
local _ticks=$(( _grace * 10 )) _i=0
while (( _i < _ticks )); do
    kill -0 -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || return 0
    sleep 0.1 2>/dev/null || true
    _i=$(( _i + 1 ))
done
```
These sleep 0.1 calls should get captured by the fake sleep binary, and the watchdog's own sleep call should log 5400 too, so I'm trying to figure out why that value isn't showing up in the log. I need to trace through the execution flow again, starting from the set -m call in lifecycle.sh and following how the hook subshell forks and sources things.

Both the hook subprocess and watchdog subprocess need to start bash, run set +m, and then do their actual work—the hook sources the plugin and runs zbuild_run, while the watchdog execs sleep with the timeout value. So this really comes down to a race condition: does the watchdog manage to exec sleep before the hook process has already finished and exited?

So the watchdog path needs an extra fork for the fake sleep binary, while the hook path avoids that since sourcing doesn't fork - it just reads and executes in place. That means the hook subshell only forks once total: for the subshell itself, then source and call `zbuild_run` with no additional process creation.

This makes the hook's bottleneck purely disk I/O for reading plugin.sh, which should be near-instant with warm page cache since the file is only a few bytes. I'm starting to suspect this test is inherently racy, though it was presumably designed to be deterministic.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
# ║  plugin-registry — lifecycle hook dispatch + fail-closed output scanner    ║
# ╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
#
# Split from registry.sh (#364). Owns the runtime dispatch path:
# `plugin_hook_call` (sources plugin.sh in an isolated subshell, applies
# pre-source tamper checks, calls the hook function, then verifies declared
# outputs) and `scan_plugin_outputs` (ADR-001 fail-closed artifact-presence
# scanner). Depends on yaml_get / verify_plugin_for_source from the other two
# split modules — sourced together via the registry.sh facade.
# Sourced library: inherits caller's pipefail settings; do not add set -euo pipefail.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_REGISTRY_LIFECYCLE_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_REGISTRY_LIFECYCLE_LOADED=1

# #1809 (ADR-058 C9): declared-output path resolution is shared with
# core/pipeline/write-boundary.sh so the artifact scanner and the write-boundary
# classifier can never disagree about where a declared output lives.
# shellcheck source=output-paths.sh
source "$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/output-paths.sh"
# shellcheck source=write-ownership.sh
source "$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/write-ownership.sh"
# shellcheck source=attempt-archive.sh
source "$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/attempt-archive.sh"
# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/stage-dispatch-mark.sh
source "$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)/scripts/lib/stage-dispatch-mark.sh"

# ─── scan_plugin_outputs — fail-closed artifact-presence scanner (#288) ─────
# ADR-001 §Fail-closed scanner contract:
#   "If a plugin declares an output but no artifact exists at outputs[].path
#    after run completes with exit 0, the engine emits a synthetic blocking
#    finding."
# #1906 retired provides.artifact_type, which the original wording keyed on;
# outputs[].required is the single declaration the scan now honours.
#
# Arguments:
#   $1 — plugin_dir
#   $2 — state_file (so $state_dir / $artifacts_dir can substitute into paths)
#
# Returns:
#   0 if all declared outputs are present (or no outputs declared).
#   1 if any declared output is missing — and emits one
#      `plugin.artifact.missing` event per missing path.
#
# Path-template substitution (Phase 0.5): supports ${state_dir} and
# ${artifact_dir} / ${artifacts_dir}. Any other ${VAR} resolves from the work
# unit's exported environment (#1803) — per-member outputs such as review-lens's
# `lens-${ZBUILD_REVIEW_LENS_ID}.json` (ADR-047 §2) are only checkable once the
# element var is expanded. A var that is unset stays literal and fails the check.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lib/stage-dispatch-mark.sh — when a stage's latest run started, and
# whether a result was written by it (ADR-068 §8).
#
# The engine never deletes a stage's output. So a stage that runs again and
# writes nothing leaves its previous result in place, and every reader must not
# take that result as this run's. One writer and one check, so no reader can
# decide it differently: _verdict_read_result, the stage report, build_kind and
# gate-aggregator all ask stage_result_is_current.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STAGE_DISPATCH_MARK_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_STAGE_DISPATCH_MARK_LOADED=1

# stage_dispatch_mark_path <state_dir> <stage>
stage_dispatch_mark_path() {
    printf '%s/runtime/dispatched/%s' "$1" "${2//[^A-Za-z0-9._-]/_}"
}

# stage_dispatch_mark <state_file> <stage> — record that <stage> starts a run
# now. Fail-open: a stage is never refused over bookkeeping.
stage_dispatch_mark() {
    local state_file="${1:-}" stage="${2:-}" m
    [[ "$state_file" == /* && -n "$stage" ]] || return 0
    m="$(stage_dispatch_mark_path "$(dirname "$state_file")" "$stage")"
    mkdir -p "${m%/*}" 2>/dev/null && : > "$m" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}
